Embodied Experimental Philosophy

Stealing Fire · Practice · Main 18 / 19

Examine continued use: revise realization, personal understanding, or philosophy, distinguishing improvements to arrangements from development of human capabilities.

An arrangement looks clear on the page. Someone lives through it, and a small hesitation changes the question. A revised question gives the next arrangement another shape. The world has entered the argument.

The preceding account has formed a usable personal arrangement, and The trinity of philosophy, psychology, and engineering explains how it is sustained across actual life, source, and works. This essay examines its consequences: as the arrangement continues in use, which changes call for modifying tools, which alter understanding of person or counterpart, and which reach the original philosophy and developmental purpose?

Philosophy gives practice concepts, images, and reasons; the person encounters the arrangement they organize through perception, attention, effort, action, and other people's responses. Continue the reading example: direct passage access may make reading easier but impede grasping the whole with another kind of material. The participants must consider new use alongside the purposes, models, and design it encounters to locate the needed change. A new trajectory thereby returns the formed way of living to reflection.

Embodied experimental philosophy names the proposal developed here: construct a meaningful arrangement, participate in it, and let its consequences inform both its realization and the philosophy guiding it. The bodily life of the person gives the inquiry a concrete situation. Experiment gives a proposed relation a way to meet something beyond its own coherence. Reflection develops what that encounter warrants and what should change next.

Participation and explanation

Participating in a practice and explaining it ask different questions. A reader may understand a theory of attention yet discover through using an interface that its explanations arrive at an exhausting rhythm. Someone else may use the same interface easily while remaining unable to explain why. Experience can disclose a relevant distinction; investigation can examine its conditions and develop an explanation.

Dewey's Reconstruction in Philosophy connects experience with acting and undergoing the consequences of action, and argues for an operative, experimental philosophy [1]. This supplies a philosophical starting point. Here its contemporary development concerns model-supported work: an idea can become a prompt, a role, an interface, or software, giving participation and explanation a common object through which to inform each other.

Embodiment makes the conditions of understanding part of the inquiry. Time, attention, perception, and the capacity to act affect what someone can take up. An explanation may need another expression when it cannot be followed during use; surprising ease may suggest a relation the theory has missed. These observations give investigation something to explain.

The model can carry implementation and investigation while the person understands through the resulting work, contributes experience, and redirects the inquiry. From personal philosophy to personal models explains how representations and contextual roles connect these contributions. Their division follows the purpose. Learning a particular skill may require exercising it; understanding and using a work can warrant a different division.

Intuition proposes; consequences distinguish

An intuition can recognize a mismatch before a full explanation is available. Perhaps repeated questions interrupt the work; perhaps an autonomous action misses a choice only the person could make. Each perception opens competing interpretations. The problem may involve wording, timing, a missing fact, a tool's behavior, or an inappropriate allocation of responsibility.

Abduction proposes an explanation that would make the observations intelligible. Reasoning unfolds its consequences. A small construction can then make the important difference encounterable. If the hypothesis concerns timing, changing only the wording may leave it unexamined. If it concerns responsibility, a new interface may succeed because it changes who makes a decision. Explicit relations help the experiment discriminate rather than merely produce another impressive output.

The consequence must bear on the claim. If fewer interruptions improve a task, that supports the arrangement's usefulness under those conditions. It does not yet show whether timing, wording, or responsibility caused the improvement, or whether the person developed a new ability. To distinguish those claims, examine cases where the candidate explanations predict different outcomes. A valid derivation unfolds premises; experience helps judge their fit to the phenomenon. Either the explanation or the way it was examined can need revision.

When a self-description becomes part of the event

A revisable personal interpretation brings another involvement into view. Suppose someone reads an account connecting their difficulty beginning with fear of evaluation. Recognizing the account, resisting it, or trying to act through it can each change what happens next. An apparent confirmation may partly reflect the attention the description directs; a changed response may reveal a possibility it helped open. Inquiry therefore considers what the account said, how it was received, what arrangement followed, and what actually happened. Those relations help distinguish an earlier pattern from a pattern partly formed through describing it.

Philosophical and psychological questions remain connected here. Clarifying that supported action can count as one's own changes a criterion of agency. Whether a particular support reduces hesitation or permits sustained activity is a question about its actual effects. The person may accept the distinction yet find the support exhausting, or use the support successfully while rejecting the proposed explanation of their hesitation. These differences give revision a direction: reconsider the picture of agency, the psychological interpretation, or the arrangement according to what the encounter reveals. The life affected by the account keeps contributing evidence and objections that its initial prose could not anticipate.

Rereading one's patterns: philosophical reflection and loosening fantasy

This section borrows psychoanalytic concepts for philosophical discussion. Personal rereading is limited to organizing experience, articulating questions, and increasing self-understanding. It supplies no method for self-help psychological analysis, assessment, treatment, or traversal of fantasy. Mental health concerns call for assessment by qualified professionals. See the use notice.

Once a personal arrangement becomes stable and usable, a further question remains: what does it enable to continue? It may support understanding, creation, and life, while also making a repeatedly constraining relationship easier to sustain. Forming a sinthome therefore opens further work: examining both how the arrangement functions and how the person participates in it.

This inquiry first returns to personal material and its maintained interpretations under references/personal/. This is the entrance for understanding one's own psychology: it brings experiences, expression, relationships, and earlier attempts to understand them together. Read the adopted personal philosophy, then recover relevant recent material from Computer History, conversations, and other histories. Add what is missing and correct inaccurate or outdated interpretations there. Which descriptions still fit experience? Which concepts and values have revealed new questions? Philosophy helps examine these interpretations, while experience can change the philosophy. Neither an earlier record nor a coherent explanation settles what the person is like.

One direction of rereading begins with recurring experiences and relational patterns in this material. How does the person meet the world and others? Whose recognition do they expect, what do they interpret as rejection, what do they believe they must become, and how do their actions help sustain these expectations? Borrowing Lacan's questions about fantasy, the inquiry concerns a relational scene organizing experience and desire, and the position the person occupies within it. Fantasy can appear as a recurrent expectation organizing relationships: what must I become for the other to give me a place? Its function needs to be understood through particular experiences.

Suppose, for example, someone repeatedly believes that a relationship will last only if they keep proving useful. Philosophical rereading can ask how personal worth relates to usefulness and whether rest belongs to a life they value. Relational inquiry further asks what judge they imagine the other to be, what position they occupy, and how continual giving, testing, and explaining help reproduce this scene. Actual demands, material dependencies, past experiences, and present expectations need comparison. Repetition opens an inquiry whose explanation remains unsettled.

The connected practical direction asks how that renewed understanding should change cooperation. The six files under references/situated/ are personal working models: orientation, person, counterpart, relationship, environment, and revision organize person–model collaboration and fit the environment to the person's psychology, purposes, and circumstances. The person file selects understanding relevant to that work; the fuller psychological inquiry remains with the personal material. After refreshing that material, condense it together with the adopted philosophy into the six working files, enact the needed environment changes, and check actual fit. For example, an old account may attribute difficulty beginning to fear of evaluation, while recent events show that an intrusive interface interrupts an otherwise willing start. Correct the interpretation in the personal references, then revise the working account and interface accordingly. An easier start supports the arrangement's usefulness; it does not certify a psychological explanation.

Philosophically, treating a requirement as a questionable premise makes other ways of participating conceivable. That possibility does not establish a change in an actual psychological process. Ordinary use can revise files, tools, and working arrangements from explicit purposes and preferences. Explanations of psychological mechanisms, distress, or relational change remain questions for discussion; they do not justify self-directed intervention or treating later changes as therapeutic effects.

The personal interpretations and working files themselves participate in this examination. An account saying “this is who I am” may summarize experience or fix a provisional interpretation as an identity. The model's explanation may repeat premises both participants share. Reading it with particular events, exceptions, and later changes keeps it open to correction. Philosophy can also become the object of reflection: an apparently higher ideal may give an old self-demand a more elaborate expression.

Lacan's traversal of fantasy and his later work on the sinthome supply connected but distinct resources. Their relation remains differently interpreted in scholarship. Here they inform philosophical examination of concepts, allowing an understanding of relational position and the construction of sustainable arrangements to revise one another. See Coffman's discussion of this unfinished relation. An insight, agreement, or document revision establishes its particular result; traversal in a clinical sense and lasting change in a life each involve further processes to understand.

These directions can interweave: philosophy makes a repetition questionable, while experience within that repetition calls the philosophy into question. The files supply revisitable accounts; life supplies what they have yet to understand. Sustaining a livable arrangement and changing one's relation to it can consequently continue within the same practice.

Two connected loops

A practice loop connects a situated proposal, its realization, participation, and correction. A reflection loop revisits how the activity is understood: which concepts and purposes organize it, what supports an explanation, and what an alternative would change. It works with a current question and standards, drawing on philosophical argument, engineering investigation, or empirical inquiry as needed. These names organize this proposal rather than defining the technical traditions of double-loop learning or second-order cybernetics.

Practice can change an interface after one concrete failure. Reflection can ask whether that failure depended on the task, presentation, or person's circumstances. It may compare cases or construct a more explicit model. Its findings can return to the practical arrangement. Practice also changes as reflection proceeds, so an earlier result has conditions and a history rather than an unlimited guarantee.

The investigator participates too. An explanation changes what a reader notices; a tool changes what a person can do; asking a question can change the response. The inquiry therefore needs relevant records of its own interventions, not only the results it receives. Describing this involvement helps distinguish a change in the practice from a change in our understanding of it.

“Experimental” here includes philosophical experimentation through making, participation, and reflection. Contemporary experimental philosophy also has a specific empirical research tradition: Knobe and Nichols describe systematic studies of the processes behind philosophical intuitions [2]. Such research can contribute where its methods fit. Trying a personal arrangement and receiving a response constitute a more local achievement.

Reasoning outside the current double-loop arrangement

Both loops and their relation can themselves become objects of inquiry. Improving practice under an existing question, or reflection under its accepted standards, leaves some organizing choices in place. Reasoning outside the current double-loop arrangement asks what justifies those choices: why divide the activities this way, what should count as evidence, and which purposes should guide reflection? It can revise the reflection loop, reconnect it with practice, or replace the arrangement.

A formal or computational system gives an inquiry selected objects, rules, states, and possible transitions. Such selection makes reasoning tractable. Ashby's account of coupling and circular influence explains feedback among parts of a dynamic system [3]; dynamic logic makes actions and changing states objects of formal reasoning [5]. These are resources for understanding work within a selected system. The present proposal also makes that selection, including the reflective arrangement through which it is assessed, available for reconsideration. This further move is the essay's philosophical proposal, rather than a claim established by those technical accounts.

Suppose an assistant maximizes completed outputs, while a reflection loop compares ways of improving that measure. Better scheduling changes practice; a better comparison changes reflection. The whole arrangement may nevertheless keep filling the person's day with work they no longer want. Taking a standpoint outside this pair allows the person and model to question why output count organizes both loops, whether the practice–reflection division serves this life, and what kinds of experience should inform judgment. They can then change the reflection loop's purpose, evidence standards, or relation to practice, as well as the assistant's behavior. The revised arrangement meets the world again through its consequences.

“Outside” is relative to the framework currently being examined. This reasoning still draws on situated experience, language, other representations, and the world. It supplies no position outside every possible framework, and it need not be installed as a fixed third loop that would become another unquestioned enclosure. What matters is keeping the current organization available for judgment and transformation.

Carnap's distinction between questions within a linguistic framework and the practical choice of a framework offers a neighboring resource [4]. Here that comparison helps distinguish inquiry using an arrangement from inquiry that reconsiders the arrangement, including its reflection loop. Connecting this distinction to intervention and consequences is the present proposal; the comparison does not by itself establish how any particular revision will work.

Eternal recurrence and returning to the loops

Practice, reflection, and reconsideration of their arrangement form a movement one can enter at different points. A practical encounter may call for inquiry; inquiry may change its own purposes or standards; that revision returns to practice. If this outward-and-returning movement is drawn as a third loop, it too remains revisable. There is no final ascent after which participation and questioning become unnecessary.

Nietzsche's eternal recurrence gives this movement a question about living. In The Gay Science §341, a demon announces the return of the same life, in the same sequence, with every pain and joy. Nietzsche asks how someone would receive that prospect and what it would take to desire it [6]. In Thus Spoke Zarathustra, III, “The Convalescent,” §2, the animals' song of circular return meets Zarathustra's account of the suffering the thought has cost him. Describing a circle and bearing its return are different achievements.

Here the connection is an authorial extension: experimental returns permit changes, whereas Nietzsche's demon announces the recurrence of the same. His question brings the life sustained by the loops into view. Could one affirm a life that includes acting, questioning, revising, and beginning again, with its difficulty as well as its joy? In the output-count example, this question can disclose why a more efficient arrangement still gives the person little reason to welcome another day within it. It can lead outside the current pair to reconsider what makes the activity worth returning to, then back into either loop with a changed purpose. A finished work, rest, and leaving a practice can all belong to the life under consideration. Returning need not make every task endless; it keeps the relation between a way of working and a life worth affirming open to encounter and judgment.

A public work as a concrete experiment

Consider a hypothetical philosophical essay published on the Web from a maintained GitHub source. A reader follows its diagram and finds that a crucial arrow seems to express causation although the text intended analogy. Their correction gives the author and model a specific difference to examine. They revise the relation, its explanation, and the diagram at the source, then check the website's rendered result. If the same misunderstanding shaped an assistant's conduct, they also revise the affected instructions and inspect actual behavior.

The published work has acquired enough independence to be understood in a way its makers did not predict. That difference is evidence about the expression; its further implications depend on whether the same relation organizes actual practice. The trinity of philosophy, psychology, and engineering situates these returns within the connection of philosophy, psychology, and engineering.

When someone chooses to share a work on WeChat Moments, responses can likewise disclose a question or an unexpected interpretation. Such a circle supplies situated clues, with silence open to several explanations, rather than a representative sample of society.

Finish a version, leave room for return

A coherent version gives something real to encounter. Quick iteration works when each version preserves the relations needed for its purpose, and checks address the uncertainty that could materially change the result. Waiting for a total theory can prevent the very encounters needed to develop it; publishing an unexamined construction can simply spread its mistake. A usable version and proportionate verification connect speed with learning.

Completion and revisability support each other. A work can be finished for its present purpose, then revised when a new question or consequence gives reason. The personal-first argument explains why a person's developing understanding and agency orient that work.

The experimental ambition is to give philosophy contact: let reasons become arrangements, let arrangements enter embodied life, and let what happens return as material for understanding. The world contributes to the argument through consequences that neither person nor model can settle by agreement.

This returns to the purpose opening Stealing fire and cultivating creative capacity. An environment becoming easier to use is a concrete improvement; recognizing new relations, asking new questions, or initiating new works in later reading, expression, and creation can further show what cultivation has accomplished. Effective supports can remain constituents of that capacity. Works and methods worth sharing enter the next essay, Adopt, combine, or create: one's practice becomes a resource others can examine, while new encounters bring different questions back.

Sources and scope

The two-loop organization and examples are this essay's synthesis, not reports of completed experiments or a general demonstration of model-assisted human development.

  1. John Dewey (1920), Reconstruction in Philosophy, especially chapters IV–V. Original text. Acting, undergoing, and operative philosophical inquiry.
  2. Joshua Knobe and Shaun Nichols (2008), An Experimental Philosophy Manifesto, pp.3–14 in Experimental Philosophy. Author-hosted proof. The distinct contemporary empirical tradition; the linked file is an uncorrected proof.
  3. W. Ross Ashby (1956), An Introduction to Cybernetics, chapter 4, especially §4/11. Estate-authorized text. Coupling and feedback within dynamic systems.
  4. Rudolf Carnap (1950), Empiricism, Semantics, and Ontology. Public reprint. Framework-relative inquiry and practical framework adoption, used here as a philosophical comparison.
  5. David Harel, Dexter Kozen, and Jerzy Tiuryn (2000), Dynamic Logic. Author's introduction. Formal reasoning about programs and their effects on states.
  6. Friedrich Nietzsche, The Gay Science (1882), §341, and Thus Spoke Zarathustra (1883–1885), III, “The Convalescent,” §2. The Gay Science, Thomas Common translation titled The Joyful Wisdom; Zarathustra, Thomas Common translation. The prospect of identical recurrence and the difficulty of affirming it; the connection to revisable experimental returns is this essay's extension.
